name: Priya Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a staff composer at Brightwater Music, a small production music company. That means I write the background tracks you hear under adverts, podcasts and TV shows: upbeat ukulele, tense strings, that sort of thing. I'm usually at my desk by half nine with a brief like 'hopeful corporate, ninety seconds, three edits'. Weekends I play keys in a wedding band called The Late Bloomers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the puzzle of a brief, making thirty seconds feel like a whole story. What wears me out is volume: my manager Colm wants twelve tracks a month, and a lot of them are close copies of what already sells. The band is the opposite. It's loud, sweaty and people actually cry at the first dance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently. Most of the AI music I've heard sounds like a hotel lobby. I'd post something about how a good brief still needs a human ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wouldn't be nothing for me. Brightwater already tried an AI tool for the cheapest tier of the catalogue last spring, the thirty-second stings. Even a plateau keeps that, and that's the work juniors used to learn on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on writing my twelve tracks a month. I'd use the AI stem tool now and then for cleaning demos, like I already do. And I'd put a bit more aside each month, because the sync money from that phone advert won't come twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, if I'm honest. My own job is fine in that picture, but the bottom of the catalogue is already shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the phone advert money.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago one of my tracks got picked for a phone advert, and my share was more than a year's salary. That's my cushion, sitting in a savings account. One lucky advert paid for my safety net, and I know I'll never get that lucky twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Brightwater, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, the junior who started in March. He was hired to do exactly those short stings. In a plateau he'd probably keep his job, but he'd have less to learn from.

say: I'd say most AI music sounds like a **hotel lobby** and a brief still needs a human ear.
I'd remind people we were told this would **change everything**, and it didn't.
think: The **cheapest tracks** in our catalogue are already going to an AI tool.
The plateau keeps my job safe but takes away the **learning work** juniors start on.
do: Keep writing **twelve tracks** a month at Brightwater and playing weekend weddings.
Save a little more each month, because the **sync money** won't come twice.
feel: **Uneasy**, because her own job is fine but the bottom of the catalogue is shrinking.
S0.quote: One lucky advert paid for my safety net, and I know I'll never get that lucky twice.
fieldNote: Priya's **cushion** comes from one lucky advert placement, and she knows it was luck.
Even in a plateau, routine **production music** is already being automated at her firm.
She worries about **juniors** like Jonah more than herself here.

steps.text: Keep writing twelve library tracks a month for Brightwater
Move a set amount each month into the sync savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the production music industry is about to be gutted, and I'd say who did it: the catalogue owners who sold old tracks to train these tools. I'd sign every petition the musicians' union puts out. I'd also say it online, because composers like me are invisible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is mostly gone within three years. Colm won't need twelve tracks from me when a tool can make a hundred 'hopeful corporate' cues by lunchtime. Maybe they keep one composer to fix and polish, and it might not be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now by getting good at the AI tools Brightwater buys, so I'm the one who supervises them, not the one let go. At the same time I'd take every wedding gig the band can get and start giving piano lessons on Thursday evenings. And I'd look into music therapy training, because I've been curious about it since uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like watching a slow tide come in when you've parked your car on the sand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the tools while signing petitions against them. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, it's awkward. I think the training was unfair and should be paid for, and I also need a job next year. I can sign the petition at lunch and still learn the software that afternoon, because my rent is due either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if your salary goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, probably. I rent a one-bedroom on my own near the station, and I'd move in with my friend Saskia to halve the rent. The savings would stay untouched as long as I could manage it.

say: I'd say production music is being **gutted** by catalogue owners who sold tracks for training.
I'd sign every **union petition** and say it online, because composers like me are invisible.
think: I think my **staff job** is mostly gone within three years.
Brightwater might keep **one composer** to polish AI tracks, and it might not be me.
do: Learn the **AI tools** Brightwater buys, aiming to supervise them rather than be replaced.
Take every **wedding gig** and start Thursday evening piano lessons.
Look into **music therapy** training she's been curious about since university.
feel: **Sick**, like watching the tide come in around a car parked on the sand.
S1.quote: I can sign the petition at lunch and still learn the software that afternoon, because my rent is due either way.
fieldNote: Priya's main income is **pure thinking work** in AI terms, so Steady Disruption hits her directly.
She holds **two positions** at once: opposing how the tools were trained and learning them anyway.
She'd protect her **savings** by cutting rent first.

steps.text: Learn Brightwater's AI music tools to become the one who supervises them
Start Thursday evening piano lessons and take every band wedding
Sign musicians' union petitions on paying for training data
Move in with Saskia to halve the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government response now, not in five years: income support for people whose work disappears, and a tax on the companies that profit. I'd be loud about it. Lots of my friends would be in the same boat, so I wouldn't feel alone saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Brightwater lets me go in 2028 or shortly after, and I'd be one of thousands of composers looking for the same few jobs. The band and the teaching are hands-on, so they'd buy me time until about 2031. After that I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Colm early and ask for a redundancy payment rather than wait. Then I'd go all in on the band and teaching, maybe twenty piano students. I'd apply for the music therapy course that same year, because therapy is about being in a room with a person, and that's the last thing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be up at two in the morning doing sums on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How long the savings last if I only have wedding and teaching money. I think about eighteen months at my current spending, two years if I move in with Saskia. Two years of savings sounds like a lot until you realise AGI also arrives in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, and I'd tell my dad the truth, because he worries less. My mum always wanted me to be a pharmacist. I don't want to give her the chance to say it.

say: I'd call for **income support** now and a tax on companies that profit from AGI.
I'd speak up loudly, because many **friends** would be in the same boat.
think: I expect Brightwater to **let me go** in 2028, along with thousands of composers.
The **band and teaching** buy me time until about 2031, then I don't know.
do: Ask Colm early for a **redundancy payment** instead of waiting to be cut.
Grow piano teaching to **twenty students** and play every band booking.
Apply for the **music therapy** course in 2028.
feel: **Scared**, awake at two in the morning doing sums on her phone.
S2.quote: Two years of savings sounds like a lot until you realise AGI also arrives in two years.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her salary**, so her strong savings soften but don't remove the alarm.
She sees the **hands-on** parts of music, teaching and playing, as a three-year bridge.
Therapy appeals because it's **human contact**, which she sees as the last thing to change.

steps.text: Negotiate a redundancy payment from Brightwater before cuts start
Grow private piano teaching to twenty students
Apply for a music therapy training course in 2028
Campaign for income support funded by a tax on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and we should use them, with proper retraining money for creative workers. I'd push the union to talk about it now rather than when the job cuts start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job still goes, but probably around 2030, and I'd see it coming. Five years is enough to finish a therapy qualification part-time. That changes things a lot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time music therapy course next autumn, paid from the sync savings. I'd keep my Brightwater job as long as it lasts and learn their AI tools so I'm useful in the meantime. And I'd keep the band, because that money is steady and it keeps me playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It feels like having a deadline rather than a car crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the course cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roughly a third of my savings over three years, I think. That's a real dent. I'd rather spend a third of my savings on a new skill than watch all of it drain while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone else in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band. Dev, our singer, writes jingles in the week, same as me. If both of us lose our day jobs, the band becomes all we've got, and that's a lot of pressure on Saturday nights.

say: I'd say we have **five years** and need retraining money for creative workers.
I'd push the **union** to plan now, before job cuts start.
think: My job still goes, but around **2030**, and I'd see it coming.
**Five years** is enough to finish a therapy qualification part-time.
do: Start a **part-time music therapy** course next autumn, paid from savings.
Keep the Brightwater job and learn its **AI tools** while it lasts.
Keep playing **weekend weddings** for steady money.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, like a deadline rather than a car crash.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend a third of my savings on a new skill than watch all of it drain while I wait.
fieldNote: Five years turns her panic into a **plan**: a part-time therapy qualification.
She'd spend about a **third of her savings**, and sees that as better than slow drain.
She notices the **band's risk** if bandmates lose their day jobs too.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time music therapy course next autumn
Learn Brightwater's AI tools well enough to stay useful
Keep playing keys with The Late Bloomers every weekend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments actually use it. I'd want a public plan for creative workers, and I'd say that at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at thirty-seven. By then I could be a qualified music therapist with a few years of practice. My composing career would be over, I think, but I'd have chosen what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brightwater for a few more years and save hard. I'd start the therapy course in two years, not straight away, once I've built the savings back up. I'd also use the AI tools more at work, because my output would go up and Colm would keep me longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit sad that composing for a living might be something I did in my twenties and then stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait two years to start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can. With ten years, I'd rather keep earning a full salary and build the savings back up first. With ten years of warning, I can leave composing on my own terms instead of being pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still compose, for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, always. I'd write songs for the band, maybe for friends' weddings. That part doesn't need to pay.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift if governments use it well.
I'd ask for a **public plan** for creative workers at every union meeting.
think: By thirty-seven I could be a qualified **music therapist** with real practice.
My **composing career** would likely be over, but I'd have chosen what comes next.
do: Stay at Brightwater a few more years and **save hard** to rebuild the cushion.
Start the **therapy course** in two years, once savings are back up.
Use the **AI tools** more at work so Colm keeps her longer.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with sadness that composing might be just a chapter of her twenties.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, I can leave composing on my own terms instead of being pushed out.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, she still expects her **composing income** to end, which keeps her anxious.
The extra time lets her **sequence** things: save first, then retrain.
She'd keep **writing songs** for love even when it stops paying.

steps.text: Save hard from the Brightwater salary for two more years
Start music therapy training in 2028 once savings recover
Use Brightwater's AI tools daily to raise monthly track output

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The two-year one is the only one where I don't have time to finish retraining before the work goes. What would help is income support while I retrain, and some kind of payment for composers whose tracks trained these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the music. All the tracks I wrote at Brightwater (the music company she works for) belong to the company, so if they sell the catalogue to train a machine, I get nothing. I think a lot of composers don't realise that yet.

headlineQuote: All the tracks I wrote at Brightwater (the music company she works for) belong to the company, so if they sell the catalogue to train a machine, I get nothing.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** staff composer writing production music, and plays keys in a wedding band.
Her **savings** came from one lucky advert placement, and she knows it won't repeat.
She's **progressive** and backs union campaigns, yet learns AI tools because her rent is due.
She expects her **composing job** to go in every scenario except the plateau.
Her way out is **music therapy**, and the warning time decides when she can start it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she couldn't finish retraining before her work disappears.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while she retrains, and payment for composers whose tracks trained the tools.
